title: Classic Adventure
build: Single-file disk transfer of the tape release: CLASSIC ADV. on a disk named DIGITAL DUNGEON 98, with a relocating wrapper

High byte of lookup_word's count of vocabulary entries tried.

Lines printed since the last command or page; the pager stops at 20.
The count of objects in the building that act_score makes; 15 sets flag 12.

The KERNAL's jiffy clock, lowest byte, counting sixtieths of a second; the chance condition reads its low seven bits.

High byte of the word number, or of travel's exit pointer.

The end of read_line's buffer, high byte.

The BASIC line the file starts with, 0 SYS 2079:" followed by eight DEL characters and UPERSOFT, so that LIST shows only 0 SUPERSOFT. RUN calls wrapper_move at 2079, $081F, which checks that the U at $0814 is still there.
The U of the hidden UPERSOFT text in the BASIC line, which wrapper_move checks before it jumps on: with the stub altered the machine hangs.

The disk transfer's wrapper, first half, run by SYS 2079 at the address the file loads to. It copies 128 pages, $0800-$87FF, up by $0340 to $0B40-$8B3F, top page first so the overlapping copy is safe, by decrementing the high bytes of its own LDA and STA operands each pass: the snapshot shows them as $0700 and $0A40 because the loop has finished. It then hangs unless $0814 still holds the U of the hidden UPERSOFT text, and jumps to wrapper_start, the moved copy of its second half.
The high byte of wrapper_move's LDA operand, $87 as loaded and decremented after each page; $07 in the snapshot, after the last.
The high byte of wrapper_move's STA operand, $8A as loaded, decremented with the source; $0A in the snapshot.

The wrapper's second half, reached in its moved copy: screen on with 25 rows ($D011 = $1B), CIA 2 timer A stopped ($DD0E = 0), $01 = $36 (BASIC ROM out, KERNAL and I/O in), the KERNAL's default I/O vectors copied from $FD36 back into $031A-$0327, interrupts on, then jump to start. The tape release's own entry was this address: the stub's text says SYS 2974.
The objects' starting locations and flags, 156 bytes: init_screen copies them here from $8AA2 before play, act_another_game copies them back for a new game, and SAVE writes them in its second file.
Three spaces before the line buffer. No instruction reads or writes them; SAVE and RESTORE carry them with the rest of the block from $0BBB.
The base the clearing loop in flush_line indexes from, with X from $2C down to 1, so its writes run from $0C85 down to $0C5A; this byte itself is never written.

The 40-column line buffer, $0C5A-$0C81, and three more bytes, $0C82-$0C84, that the clearing loop also fills with spaces: typed commands are read into it, and text is built in it a line at a time before it is justified and printed.
The column put_char writes next in the line buffer.
print_record's spacing state: 0 at the start of a line or after an apostrophe, slash or hyphen, 1 after a dictionary word, 2 after any other character.
Set when the line being built is not to be justified: the last line of a record, a line with '%', the pager's line.
1 while the status rules run, 0 for the command rules: says where run_actions goes when a rule's actions run out.
1 when the last condition tested held.
Stays 1 while act_inventory has found nothing carried.
The object number act_inventory is on.
The first known word of the command, the verb or a direction; 0 for none.
The second known word, the noun; $FF for none.
The third known word; $FF for none. No rule reads it.
The word number lookup_word found, 0 for none.
The four letters of the word being looked up, zero-filled.

Flags 0 to 12, one byte each. Flag 2 is the count of objects carried, flag 5 the darkness count, flag 10 says the game is over, flag 12 that the cave is closing; flags 6 and 7 are set by pouring water and oil, 8 and 9 by the blasts, and flags 3 and 4 are counted down but never set.
Flag 2: the number of objects carried, 0 to 7, kept by act_get, act_drop and death.
Flag 3, counted down by end_turn whenever it is not 0. No rule sets it, so it stays 0.
Flag 4, counted down by describe_room in an unlit room whenever it is not 0. No rule sets it, so it stays 0.

Flag 5, the darkness count: 4 at a new game, 3 after a death, one less for each time a dark room is described. Status rule 21 kills the player when it reaches 0. Nothing raises it during a life: action 14, which would set it to 4, is used by no rule.
Flag 10, the game is over: set by QUIT, by each of the three blasts and by the last death; act_score then offers another game.
Flag 12, the cave is closing: set by act_score when exactly 15 objects lie in the building; status rules 11 and 12 then move the player to the repository from the hall of mists.
The turn count, 16 bits, counted by get_command. No instruction reads it, though SAVE and RESTORE carry it with the rest of the block from $0BBB: the score shows the ASCII copy at $0F68 instead.
High byte of the 16-bit turn count.
The player's room, 1 to 140; 0 means dead.
Set to 0 by new_game. No other instruction reads or writes it; SAVE and RESTORE carry it with the rest of the block from $0BBB.
The room the player came from; death leaves the carried objects there.

$0CA7 and $0CA8 hold rooms 21 and 22, the rooms of 'You didn't make it' and 'The dome is unclimbable', which are never remembered as the previous room. $0CA6 itself is set to 0 by new_game, and no instruction reads it; SAVE and RESTORE carry it with the rest of the block from $0BBB.
Rooms 21 and 22, which travel and act_goto never record as the previous room: status rules 2 and 3 send the player on from them at once.
Set once show_room has printed 'Here can be seen:-'.
Set by travel when an exit was taken.
The handler address that test_condition and run_actions jump through.
High byte of the handler address at $0CAB.
Lives left after this one, 4 at the start.
The 13 rooms that are lit without the lamp: 1-9, 100, 115, 116 and 126.
The rule being tried, copied with the start of the next one: 8 bytes for a status rule, 12 for a command rule, so both ends of its condition and action lists are at hand.
Byte 1 of the copied rule: the high byte of a status rule's condition offset, or a command rule's noun.
Bytes 2 and 3 of the copied rule: a status rule's action offset, or a command rule's condition offset.
Byte 3 of the copied rule, the high byte of the offset at $0CBD.
Bytes 4 and 5 of the copied rule: the next status rule's condition offset, which ends this rule's conditions, or a command rule's action offset.
Byte 5 of the copied rule, the high byte of the offset at $0CBF.
Bytes 6 and 7 of the copied rule: the next status rule's action offset, which ends this rule's actions. A command rule's copy has the next rule's verb and noun here, which nothing reads.
Byte 7 of the copied rule, the high byte of the offset at $0CC1.
Bytes 8 and 9, copied for command rules only: the next rule's condition offset, which ends this rule's conditions.
Byte 9 of a copied command rule, the high byte of the offset at $0CC3.
Bytes 10 and 11 of a copied command rule: the next rule's action offset, which ends this rule's actions.
Byte 11 of a copied command rule, the high byte of the offset at $0CC5.
parse's column in the line buffer; justify's working column.

The 20 action handlers, by action code 0-19: inventory, get, drop, message, describe, end turn, go, set flag, clear flag, another game, Okay, quit, place here, destroy, set flag to 4, score, remember room, move object to the remembered room, SAVE and RESTORE. run_actions jumps through it.

The 11 condition handlers, by condition code 0-10: in room, carried or here, chance, neither carried nor here, flag set, flag clear, carried, here, not here, not carried, has a location or flags. test_condition jumps through it.

Print dictionary word n, n in $A7/$A8 counted from 1. Walks the dictionary from $1D4C, skipping n-1 words (each ends with a byte that has bit 7 set), then sends the word's letters, bit 7 cleared, to put_char. Called by print_record for a two-byte word reference.

Put one character into the 40-column line buffer at $0C5A, at column $0C85. A carriage return instead flushes the line (flush_line) and counts it in $52; at 20 lines the pager puts 'Hit any key to continue.' through the same path (marking it not to be justified), waits until the KERNAL's key matrix code $C5 is no longer $40 (no key), empties the keyboard buffer ($C6 = 0) and starts the count again.

Justify the line buffer unless $0C87 says not to (justify), print its 40 characters through chrout_swap, then fill $0C5A-$0C85 with spaces and set the column $0C85 and the spacing state $0C86 to 0. A full 40-character line leaves the cursor at the start of the next screen row, so no carriage return is sent.
Empty the line buffer without printing it: a jump to the tail of flush_line.

Print record A (from 1) of a text table: ($97) points at a table of 16-bit offsets, ($A9) at the text they are relative to, and record n runs from offset n-1 to offset n. An empty record prints only a carriage return. Each byte below 4 starts a two-byte dictionary word number (print_word); '%' marks the line as one not to justify and prints nothing; a carriage return ends a line, and the last byte of the record being one marks that line not to be justified. A space is put before a word, and before a letter that follows a word, using $0C86 (1 after a word, 2 after a character other than an apostrophe, slash or hyphen). The record ends with an extra carriage return sent straight to the screen, which leaves a blank line, and adds 1 to the line count $52.
Part of print_record: when the carriage return just read is the record's last byte ($61/$62 down to 1), set $0C87 so that line is not justified.

CHROUT ($FFD2) with the case of letters swapped: the game's text is ASCII, and with the upper and lower case character set PETSCII has the cases the other way round, so any byte from $41 to $7F is sent with bit 5 flipped. Keeps X and Y.

Full justification of the 40-character line buffer, unless $0C87 is set. When column 39 holds a space it finds the last word, then the gap before it, and shifts the rest of the line right by one column, so a space is added at that gap; the next pass works one gap further left, wrapping round to the right-hand end, until column 39 holds a letter. Lines that end a paragraph, and text marked with '%', are left ragged.

Read a typed line through CHRIN ($FFCF), the KERNAL's screen editor, into $0C5A, at most 39 characters; the rest of a longer line is read and dropped. Prints a carriage return and sets the line count $52 to 0.

Turn the typed line into up to three word numbers: spaces become 0 and bit 7 is cleared (so shifted letters match too), then each word in turn is cut to four letters (next_word) and looked up (lookup_word). Unknown words are skipped. The first known word goes to $0C8C, the next two to $0C8D and $0C8E ($FF when there is none); $0C8C stays 0 when no word is known.
Copy the next word of the parsed line, from column $0CC7, into $0C90-$0C93: at most four letters, zero-filled; the rest of a longer word is skipped. $0C90 is 0 when the line is used up.
Find the four letters at $0C90 in the 226 five-byte entries of the vocabulary at $47DF; $0C8F gets the entry's word number, or 0 when no entry matches.
The game's first instruction, reached from the wrapper. Empties the line buffer and sets up the screen (init_screen), then falls into new_game.

Start a game: the turn count $0CA1/$0CA2 to 0 and its printed digits at $0F68 to '   0', the previous room $0CA5 and $0CA4, $0CA6 to 0, the room to 1 (the road), flags 0-12 to 0, the darkness count (flag 5) and the lives left $0CAD to 4. Another game? comes back here after restoring the objects.
Each time the room may have changed: room 0 means the player has died (death); otherwise describe the room (describe_room) and fall into the status rules.

Run the 30 status rules at $66C7 before every command. Each rule is 4 bytes, the offsets of its conditions in $6743 and of its actions in $679D, and the next rule's offsets end its lists, so the 8 bytes are copied to $0CBB. A rule whose conditions all hold runs its actions (run_actions); with $0C88 set the actions return here for the next rule, unless one of them ends the turn. After the last rule, get the next command.
Where the 'end turn' action comes: count flag 3 down if it is not 0, then get the next command without running the status rules. No rule sets flag 3.

Read and act on a command: read_line; add 1 to the turn count $0CA1/$0CA2 and to the ASCII digits of the turns at $0F68 (a space before the first digit becomes a 0 on a carry); parse; print a blank line. With no known word say 'I dont understand!' and read again. Otherwise try the room's exits (travel); a move goes back to main_loop to describe the new room. Otherwise fall into the command rules.

Scan the 422 command rules at $5209 in order. A rule is 6 bytes: verb, noun ($FF for any), and the offsets of its conditions in $5BF3 and its actions in $5FD9, which end at the next rule's offsets. A rule applies when the verb is the first word and the noun is $FF or the second word; when all its conditions hold, its actions run (run_actions), and nearly every action list ends the turn. The scan ends at the sentinel record at $5BED.

The command rules ran out, or a command rule's actions ran to their end. $0C89 still set by the last condition tested means a rule ran, and the status rules follow. Otherwise nothing matched: 'I cant', or 'I cant go that way' when the first word is a direction (words 43 to 54), then the status rules.

Describe the room, or the dark. Rooms 1-9, 100, 115, 116 and 126, listed at $0CAE, are lit; so is any room where the lit lamp (object 3) lies or while it is carried. Otherwise flag 4 is counted down when it is not 0 (no rule sets it), 'It is now pitch dark. If you proceed you will likely fall into a pit!' is printed, and the darkness count, flag 5, goes down by one; status rule 21 kills the player when it reaches 0.

Part of describe_room: print the room's text (offsets $2347, text $2461), then every object whose location is this room, in object order, under 'Here can be seen:-', printed once ($0CA9). A carried object has location 0 and is not listed.
Print 'I dont understand!'.

Try the current room's exits: the room's (word, destination) pairs, from offsets at $4C49 into $4D63. On a pair whose word is the command's first word, remember the room as the previous room $0CA5 unless it is room 21 or 22 ($0CA7, $0CA8), move to the destination and set $0CAA. The count of bytes left is tested by comparing its two bytes with each other, which works because no room has 256 bytes of exits.
Empty the line buffer and print it, a blank line.
Test one condition, code $4B with argument $4C: clear $0C89 and jump through the condition table at $0CF0; the handler sets $0C89 to 1 when the condition holds (cond_true) and returns.
Condition 0: the player is in room n.
Condition 1: object n is carried (bit 1 of its flags byte) or lies in this room.
Condition 2: chance, n in 128. Holds when the low seven bits of the KERNAL's jiffy clock $A2 are below n.
Condition 3: object n is neither carried nor in this room.
Condition 4: flag n ($0C94+n) is not 0.
Condition 5: flag n is 0.
Condition 6: object n is carried.
Condition 7: object n lies in this room. A carried object has location 0, so it does not count.
Condition 8: object n does not lie in this room; carried counts as not here.
Condition 9: object n is not carried.
Condition 10: object n's location or its flags byte is not 0. Every treasure has bit 4 set in its flags, so a treasure always passes, even one removed from play.
The condition holds: $0C89 = 1.

Run a rule's actions, read two bytes at a time, code and argument: jump through the action table at $0CC8 with the argument in $4C. The actions that ignore the argument all leave the rule, so the lists store them as the code alone and the byte read with it belongs to the next list. A handler that does not end the turn comes back to next_action. When the list runs out, a status rule goes on to the next status rule and a command rule to no_rule.
Step the action pointer $63/$64 on by 2 and the bytes left $68/$69 down by 2, and run the next action.
Action 0: 'You are carrying', then every object with bit 1 set in its flags, or 'nothing at all'; then the status rules.

Action 1, take object n: refused with 'You can't carry any more' when flag 2, the count of objects carried, is 7. An object in this room gets location 0 and bit 1 set in its flags, and the count goes up. Any other object, carried or in another room, gives 'You have it already' and ends the action list.
Action 2, drop object n: a carried object loses bit 1, takes this room as its location, and the count goes down. Otherwise 'You dont have it' ends the action list.
Action 3: print message n (offsets $6855, text $69E7), then the next action.
Action 4: describe the room again (main_loop) and run the status rules. Its argument is not read.
Action 5: end the turn without running the status rules (end_turn).
Action 6: go to room n, remembering the room left as the previous room unless it is room 21 or 22; then main_loop. Room 0 is death.
Action 7: set flag n to $FF.
Action 8: set flag n to 0.

Action 9, also reached from act_score once flag 10 says the game is over: 'Another game (y or n)?'. An unshifted N ($4E) jumps through the reset vector at $FFFC and the machine restarts into BASIC. Any other answer copies the objects' starting locations back from $0BBB and starts a new game. The test ANDs the key with $DF, which folds ASCII lower case, but a shifted N arrives as $CE and counts as yes. No rule uses the action itself.
Action 10: print 'Okay', then the status rules.
Action 11: 'Are you sure?'. An unshifted Y ($59) sets flag 10 and shows the score, which then offers another game; anything else goes on to the status rules.
Action 12: put object n in this room. Its flags byte is not changed.
Action 13: object n's location becomes 0, out of play. The carried bit is left as it was, so the rules always drop an object before destroying it.
Action 14: set flag n to 4. No rule uses it.

Action 15: count 10 for each object in the building (room 3) with bit 4, the treasure bit, in its flags, in the ASCII digits at $0F48 (a hundreds digit appears at 100). When exactly 15 objects of any kind lie in the building, set flag 12, which closes the cave. Print 'You have scored .. out of a possible 210 using .. turns.'; with flag 10 set (quit, blasted or out of lives) offer another game, otherwise run the status rules.
Action 16: remember room n in $65 for the next action 17.
Action 17: object n's location becomes the room remembered by action 16.

Action 18, SAVE: two files to tape (device 1, secondary address 1, no name). The first holds $8AA2-$8B3C, the objects' locations and flags except the last byte, object 78's flags, which nothing changes. The second holds $0BBB-$0F97: the starting locations, the line buffer and the variables, the handler tables and the built-in messages, with the turn and score digits. RUN/STOP at the tape prompt abandons the save and the game goes on.
Action 19, RESTORE: load the two files SAVE wrote, each to the address it was saved from (secondary address 1), then describe the room.
A one-record offset table for print_inline: the offsets 0 and the message length, which print_inline writes into $1ADB before each built-in message is printed.
The second offset of inline_offsets: the length of the built-in message being printed, written by print_inline.

Print X bytes from ($B6) as one record: X is written into the one-record offset table at $1AD9, which print_record then reads with ($B6) as the text base. Every built-in message at $0D06-$0F98 goes through here.

Set up the screen and save the starting state: CHROUT $0E (upper and lower case set), $08 (shift and Commodore key no longer switch the set), empty the keyboard buffer, $05 (white text), border blue ($D020 = 6), $93 (clear the screen). Copy the 156 bytes of object locations and flags at $8AA2 to $0BBB, where another game reads them back, and print the welcome text.

Room 0, death. With no lives left ($0CAD = 0) set flag 10 and show the score, which ends the game. Otherwise take a life, print the reincarnation text with the lives count before this death in its digit at $0EF0 (4 the first time), put a carried lamp (object 2 or 3) on the road, room 1, put every other carried object in the previous room $0CA5, not the room of the death, set the carried count to 0, the room to 3 (the building) and the darkness count to 3, and describe the building.

Code nothing calls or jumps to, never run: an older build of the printing routines left in memory when the program was saved. Its pieces match the live ones at an offset of $0BB8 with small differences: the pager ($1BAA, as $0FF2), the line flush and clear ($1BC7, as $100F), print_record ($1BEB, as $1033) and a CHROUT with case swap ($1CE8). Its calls point at the older build's addresses, so it is kept as bytes rather than traced.

Room 104's text: "You are in a long sloping corridor with ragged sharp walls."
Room 105's text: "You are in a cul-de-sac about eight feet across."

Room 106's text: "You are in an ante-room leading to a large passage to the east. Small passages go west and up. The remnants of recent digging are evident. A sign in midair here says 'Cave under construction beyond this point. Proceed at own risk. ( Witt Construction Company)'."
Room 107's text: "You are in a maze of twisty little passages, all different."
Room 108's text: "You are at Witt's end. Passages lead off in * all* directions."

Room 109's text: "You are in a N/S canyon about 25 feet across. The floor is covered by white mist seeping in from the north. The walls extend upward for well over 100 feet. Suspended from some unseen point far above you, an enormous two-sided mirror is hanging parallel to and midway between the canyon walls. ( The mirror is obviously provided for the use of the dwarves, who as you know, are extremely vain.) A small window can be seen in either wall, some fifty feet up."

Room 111's text: "A large stalactite extends from the roof and almost reaches the floor below. You could climb down it, and jump from it to the floor, but having done so you would be unable to reach it to climb back up."
Room 112's text: "You are in a little maze of twisting passages, all different."

Room 113's text: "You are at the edge of a large underground reservoir. An opaque cloud of white mist fills the room and rises rapidly upward. The lake is fed by a stream, which tumbles out of a hole in the wall about 10 feet overhead and splashes noisily into the water somewhere within the mist . The only passage goes back toward the south."
Room 114's text: "Dead end."

Room 115's text: "You are at the northeast end of an immense room, even larger than the giant room. It appears to be a repository for the 'Adventure' program. Massive torches far overhead bathe the room with smoky yellow light. Scattered about you can be seen a pile of bottles ( all of them empty), a nursery of young beanstalks murmuring quietly, a bed of oysters, a bundle of black rods with rusty stars on their ends, and a collection of brass lanterns. An immense mirror is hanging against one wall, and stretches to the other end of the room where various other sundry objects can be glimpsed dimly in the distance."

On the other side is a row of small wicker cages, each of which contains a little sulking bird. In one corner is a bundle of black rods with rusty marks on their ends. A large number of velvet pillows are scattered about on the floor. A vast mirror stretches off to the northeast. At your feet is a large steel grate, next to which is a sign which reads, 'Treasure vault. Keys in main office.'."
Room 117's text: "You are on one side of a large deep chasm. A heavy white mist rising up canyon below obscures all view of the far side. A SW path leads away from the chasm into a winding corridor."

Room 123's text: "You are in a long east/west corridor. A faint rumbling noise can be heard in the distance."

Room 124's text: "The path forks here. The left fork leads northeast. A dull rumbling seems to get louder in that direction. The right fork leads southeast down a gentle slope. The main corridor enters from the west."

Room 125's text: "The walls are quite warm here. From the north can be heard a steady roar, so loud that the entire cave seems to be trembling. Another passage leads south, and a low crawl goes east."

Room 126's text: "You are on the edge of a breath-taking view. Far below you is an active volcano, from which great gouts of molten lava come surging out, cascading back down into the depths. A river of fire crashes out from the depths of the volcano and plummets into a bottomless pit far off to your left. To the right, an immense geyser of blistering steam erupts continuously from a barren island in the center of a sulfurous lake, which bubbles ominously. The far right wall is aflame with an incandescence of its own, which lends an additional infernal splendor to the already hellish scene. A dark, foreboding passage exits to the south."

Room 127's text: "You are in a small chamber filled with large boulders. The walls are very warm, causing the air in the room to be almost stifling from the heat. The only exit is a crawl heading west, through which is coming a low rumbling."
Room 128's text: "You are walking along a gently sloping north/south passage lined with oddly shaped limestone formations."
Room 129's text: "You are standing at the entrance to a large barren room. A sign posted above the entrance reads: 'Caution! BEAR IN ROOM!'."

Message 51's text: "I know of places, actions and things. Most of my vocabulary describes places and is used to move you there. To move, try words like forest, building, enter, east, north or up. I know about a few special objects like a black rod in the cave. These objects can be manipulated using my vocabulary. To get a list of what you're carrying use 'Inventory'. The objects have side effects; for instance the rod scares the bird. Also, note that cave passages turn a lot, and that leaving a room to the north does not guarantee entering the next from the south."
